newsitem.title: USA: Forbes seeks to shape U.S. agenda, could run again.
newsitem.headline: Forbes seeks to shape U.S. agenda, could run again.

text.p: Multi-millionaire publisher Steve Forbes, who shook up the 1996 presidential race, is behaving like a man who is seriously thinking of running for the White House again.

Forbes, who spent over $30 million of his personal fortune on his 1996 presidential bid, recently spent several million more to launch Americans for Hope, Growth and Opportunity, a issues advocacy group designed to spread his ideas on politics and economics.

In an interview with Reuters in his New York headquarters on Monday, Forbes did not rule out another presidential run in 2000 and said that if he did run again, he would be better prepared than he was last time.
"I'm not ruling anything in or anything out right now," Forbes said, adding that he would decide after the 1998 congressional elections.

His aim right now was to affect the national agenda. "Regardless of what happens to me or to other personalities, you'd have an environment where political figures would be responding to this agenda instead of operating in a vacuum as they sometimes seem to be even in Washington today," he said.
Of his 1996 bid, Forbes said he started campaigning too late to have a realistic chance of winning the Republican nomination against others who had been preparing for years.
"Starting so late was like riding a freight train while building the track at the same time," he said.
"If I ever do something like that again, or work with somebody who is going to do something like that, you must have a strategy because on the campaign trail you can't devise it as you go along."
Forbes won two early Republican primaries, in Arizona and Delaware, but lacked the nationwide organisation to exploit his victories. Still, he had a large impact on the race.

A senior aide to eventual Republican nominee Bob Dole said Forbes seriously damaged Dole with an aggressive advertisement campaign, softening him up for eventual defeat at the hands of President Bill Clinton.

Forbes' new group has already sprung into action. Last week it paid for a radio advertisement calling for an independent investigation of Democratic and White House fund raising. This week it has a spot opposing late term abortions which is running on 600 stations nationwide.
Forbes said he had provided the seed money "in the low six figures" for the group and set it up in an office with three staff. Now he is appealing for private funds to support it.

He is also travelling the country addressing Republican groups and making a special effort to mend fences with Christian conservative groups that opposed his 1996 bid. Recently he was at Liberty University in Virginia, an institution run by conservative evangelist Jerry Falwell.
He acknowledged he was not a very religious man who did not go to church as often as he should, but said he wanted to find common ground with Christian conservatives.
